episode.lensDescription: What can you DO with this? Practical, tactical, classroom-ready.
episode.broadcastScript:
Welcome to The Innovation Pulse from Innovating Higher Ed. It's Wednesday, March 4th.

A political science professor at Slippery Rock University just delivered a warning that caught my attention. He says new A.I. agents can now log into online courses and complete them entirely on their own, without any human involvement. That's not speculation about the future, that's happening right now.

-
Let me catch you up on what else is happening this week. In our Latest A.I. Products category today, the University of Houston just went all-in with Google, deploying Gemini for Education and NotebookLM to every student, faculty member, and staff person on campus. What's interesting here is the security angle. UH structured the partnership so their research data stays within the university ecosystem and doesn't get used to train Google's public A.I. models. They're calling it a way to make every graduate A.I. proficient while protecting intellectual property. Worth watching how this plays out at scale.

-
From the Case Study file, Bucks County school districts in Pennsylvania are taking wildly different approaches to A.I. integration. A new survey shows some districts have formal policies with assignment scales, others are running pilot programs, and some have created think tanks to figure it out. Central Bucks is launching a Microsoft Copilot pilot specifically for high school students, while other districts are focusing on teacher training and ethical use guidelines. It's a good snapshot of how varied the landscape still is, even within one county.

-
And here's one from our Beyond Ed category that caught my eye. JD Institute of Fashion Technology in India just partnered with something called MYTH A.I. to bring artificial intelligence tools for textile and clothing design to students across their 40-plus campuses. The platform provides digital textile libraries and garment visualization tools to speed up design ideation. Fashion design education isn't something we cover often, but it's another example of A.I. moving into hands-on creative fields.

-
Now, let's get to that story I mentioned at the top. Nicholas Spina, that political science professor at Slippery Rock, wasn't just making casual observations about A.I. in education. He was delivering a formal presentation through the university's Center for Community Engagement, and his message was pretty direct. New A.I. agents like Perplexity's Comet and ChatGPT's Atlas can log into online courses and complete them entirely without human involvement.

What makes this different from earlier concerns about A.I. and academic dishonesty is the scope. Spina isn't talking about students using A.I. to write individual essays or solve specific problems. He's describing systems that can navigate entire courses, complete assignments, participate in discussions, and submit work, all while mimicking student engagement patterns.

His central argument is this: if an assignment can be completed entirely through screen-based interaction, we need to examine whether it's actually helping students learn. That's not just a technology question, it's a fundamental course design question. And it's one that many of us are facing in real time, whether we've articulated it this way or not.

What I find particularly striking about Spina's perspective is how he frames the broader implications. He suggests that A.I.'s mere availability diminishes the perceived integrity of education, regardless of whether students actually use these tools inappropriately. That's a challenging idea. It means that even if our students are engaging authentically, the public perception of educational value might be affected by what's technically possible.

This timing matters because many institutions are still developing their A.I. policies. Slippery Rock has a task force working on this and offers resources through their Center for Teaching and Learning. But faculty are already encountering these challenges in their classrooms, often without clear institutional guidance.

For those of us teaching this week, Spina's framework offers a practical lens. Look at assignments that can be completed entirely through screen-based interaction. This doesn't necessarily mean abandoning digital tools or online components. But it does suggest thinking more deliberately about where human insight, physical presence, or collaborative interaction become essential elements of the learning process.

I keep thinking about the implications for community colleges, where budget constraints often push toward online delivery and automated assessment. These are exactly the environments where A.I. agents can operate most effectively. Students juggling multiple jobs and family responsibilities find screen-based convenience appealing, which makes sense. But if those same conveniences can be automated entirely, what are we actually offering?

Spina's point about perceived integrity feels especially relevant for institutions where credibility and workforce preparation are closely linked. Are we prepared to have honest conversations with our communities about what learning looks like when A.I. can complete assignments? And more practically, how do we design meaningful learning experiences that require the kind of thinking, synthesis, and application that genuinely benefits from human engagement?

The question isn't whether to use A.I., but how to create learning experiences where human involvement isn't just required, it's irreplaceable.

-
These aren't easy questions, but they're the ones we're grappling with right now, in real classrooms with real students. That's your Innovation Pulse for Wednesday. Find full coverage and links at innovating higher ed dot com. See you Thursday.

Dr. Norma Jones. Thanks for listening.
